clue.text: Fight French arbitrators

parts.note: standard abbreviation for French
the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service, the UK body that settles industrial disputes

explanation.surface: A row breaks out among the people from France brought in to referee a dispute.
explanation.definitionFit: A fracas is a noisy quarrel or brawl, a close synonym for a fight.

clue.text: Space dock found in ascent

indicators.note: in a down entry, something ascending is read from the bottom upwards, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: to moor a boat is to dock it

explanation.surface: Somewhere to berth a craft is located as it rises, like a spacecraft docking.
explanation.definitionFit: Room means available space, as in 'no room to move'.

clue.text: Corrupt corporate circles silence gambler

indicators.note: to circle something is to go round it, so one piece surrounds the other
something corrupt has been twisted out of its proper form, so the letters get rearranged

parts.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written
the hushing noise used to call for silence

explanation.surface: A crooked company buys off a whistleblowing gambler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt' reads as an adjective describing the firm, but it tells you to rearrange the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A crapshooter plays craps, a dice game, so is a type of gambler.

clue.text: A deep breath

parts.note: surface reading: a big lungful of air
setter's reading: the deep is the ocean, so a breath from the deep is a gentle wind off the water

explanation.walkthrough: 'The deep' is a poetic name for the ocean, so the breath is wind blowing in from it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea breeze is a light wind blowing from the ocean onto land, a breath of the deep.

clue.text: Easy goal to catch stray reptile

indicators.note: catching something means holding it inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a tap-in is a simple goal knocked in from close range
to err is to stray from the right path

explanation.surface: A footballer's simple close-range finish manages to trap a wandering animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrapin is a small freshwater turtle, which is a reptile.

clue.text: Tango's fashionable, and it's awful

parts.note: Tango is T in the NATO alphabet; the 's only serves the surface
an old slang word for stylish, an earlier form of hip
taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A dance critic grumbles that the tango is trendy but dreadful.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The pits' is an idiom for the worst possible, used as a predicate meaning awful.

clue.text: Hotel not to put up prince or king

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something up lifts it so it reads from the bottom upwards

parts.note: Hotel is H in the NATO alphabet
a door that is 'to' is shut, so one not to is ajar

explanation.surface: A hotel refuses to give rooms to visiting royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' here is the British use for a door pushed closed; a door not to is slightly open.
explanation.definitionFit: A rajah is an Indian ruler, whose rank covers both a prince and a king.

clue.text: One extremely fat behind

parts.note: a means one

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its first and last letters are kept

parts.note: the two end letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone has an extremely large rear end.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'behind' as a backside; it is the nautical direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Aft is the sailor's word for behind or towards the stern.

clue.text: Might I turn minister out?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to turn the word round is to make it face the other way, so it is written backwards

parts.note: might and can both express possibility or ability
a curate is a junior Church of England minister

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether they could expel a cabinet member.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come from the clue out of order: I, then CAN turned to NAC, then CURATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A calculation that is out is wrong, which is to say inaccurate.

clue.text: Run, with another old chap, into jail

indicators.note: one piece is put into the other, so it sits inside it

parts.note: a cage is a place of confinement, slang for a prison
standard abbreviation for old
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A prisoner flees with an elderly fellow inmate into the jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' looks like an escape, but it means manage, as in running a business.
explanation.definitionFit: To co-manage is to run an organisation jointly with a partner.

clue.text: Spade placed on right of black debris on beach

indicators.note: to be on the right is to come after in a word written across, so this piece follows the other

parts.note: jet black is a deep black colour
Sam Spade is the private detective in Hammett's The Maltese Falcon

explanation.surface: A digging tool is left beside a dark heap of rubbish on the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spade' looks like a tool or a card suit; it is the detective's surname, standing for his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Jetsam is cargo thrown overboard that washes up, so it is debris found on a beach.

clue.text: Keep one of these and give nothing away

definitions.text: Keep one of these and give nothing away

parts.note: surface reading: retain some possession of yours
setter's reading: show no emotion in your expression, as when trying not to laugh

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like advice about hoarding possessions; the thing kept is an expression, and what is given away is a feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadpan look that hides your amusement or feelings is exactly what lets you reveal nothing.

clue.text: Scrappy fight involving FBI agents and sailor

indicators.note: to involve is to take in or include, so the other pieces sit inside it

parts.note: a fray is a fight or skirmish
G-men is American slang for FBI agents, short for Government men
tar is an old word for a sailor

explanation.surface: A scrappy brawl breaks out between federal agents and a seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrappy' suggests the fight; it is the definition, in its sense of bitty and disjointed.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrappy work is made of odd bits and pieces, which is to say incomplete and broken up.

clue.text: Notice coat near ceiling, as Spooner might say

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner was known for swapping the opening sounds of words, so the initial sounds trade places

parts.note: to cake is to coat thickly, and up the wall is near the ceiling; swap the opening sounds of the outer words

explanation.surface: An instruction to paint near the top of a room, or a notice pinned up high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notice' looks like a sign on the wall; it is a warning, the kind that jolts someone awake.
explanation.definitionFit: A wake-up call is a warning that jolts someone to attention, a notice in that sense.

clue.text: Pop over low part of wall

parts.note: pop is an informal word for father
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Father climbs over a short garden wall.
explanation.definitionFit: A dado is the lower section of an interior wall, often finished differently from the part above.

clue.text: Trying to sit in them might seem odd

definitions.text: Trying to sit in them might seem odd

parts.note: surface reading: making the attempt to sit down in some seats
setter's reading: 'trying' also means difficult, and these seats are the opposite of difficult

explanation.walkthrough: 'Trying' reads as attempting; it is the adjective meaning hard, the opposite of the first word of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy chairs are comfortable armchairs; finding them trying would be a contradiction.

clue.text: Landmass which is dry?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one of the world's great land areas
second meaning: self-restrained, abstaining, as a teetotaller is dry

explanation.surface: A puzzled geographer asks whether a landmass counts as dry land.
explanation.walkthrough: As an adjective the word means exercising self-restraint, and dry means abstaining from drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a large landmass such as Africa; the adjective means abstinent, as a dry person avoids alcohol.

clue.text: Met worker, Scots kid, outside The Academy

indicators.note: being outside means wrapping around, so the other pieces sit within this one

parts.note: wean is the Scots word for a small child
taken as written
the Royal Military Academy, Sandhurst

explanation.surface: A Scottish youngster works for the Met Office, near a famous institution.
explanation.walkthrough: The Met here is the UK Met Office, the national weather service, not the London police.
explanation.definitionFit: A weatherman forecasts the weather, the job of a Met Office worker.

clue.text: Laddish guards shot some soldiers once

indicators.note: to guard something is to stand around it protectively, so it holds the other piece inside

parts.note: laddish behaviour is stereotypically masculine
a nip is a small shot of spirits

explanation.surface: Young men keep watch while some soldiers fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' suggests gunfire; it is a small measure of drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A maniple was a subdivision of a Roman legion, a body of soldiers from ancient times.

clue.text: Fancy being given most of the story

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its last letter, so the end is dropped

parts.note: 'Fancy!' and 'My!' are both exclamations of surprise
the word with its last letter removed

explanation.surface: Someone imagines being handed most of a tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like a verb or adjective; it is the exclamation, as in 'Fancy that!'.
explanation.definitionFit: A myth is a traditional story, often about gods or heroes.

clue.text: The catching of butterflies

definitions.meaning: first meaning: arrest, the capture of a suspect
second meaning: anxious nerves, butterflies in the stomach

explanation.surface: A lepidopterist nets specimens.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a collector with a net; the two halves are separate meanings, arrest and nervousness.
explanation.definitionFit: Apprehension means both the arrest of a criminal and anxious dread, which is having butterflies.

clue.text: How do royals dominate its pages?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a greeting, 'how do you do'
second meaning: the celebrity magazine famous for royal coverage

explanation.surface: A puzzled reader asks how the royal family ends up taking over a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Hello! is a British celebrity and society magazine known for photo spreads of royals.
explanation.definitionFit: Hello is a greeting like 'how do'; it is also the name of the gossip weekly packed with royal stories.

clue.text: Screen around November 26?

indicators.note: one piece goes around the other, so it holds it inside

parts.note: to vet a candidate is to screen them
November is N in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A screen goes up around a date late in November.
explanation.walkthrough: '26' is not a date but a cross-reference to the answer at 26 across; the question mark flags that this is one example of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A blowhole is an outlet for air or a whale's breathing opening, which is a kind of vent.

clue.text: Artist fights depression — doesn't quite make it

indicators.note: falling just short means the word stops one letter before its end

parts.note: war is fighting between nations
a hole is a hollow or depression, here missing its last letter

explanation.surface: A painter battles low moods and never quite succeeds.
explanation.definitionFit: Andy Warhol was the American pop artist famed for his soup-can and celebrity prints.

clue.text: Fell into the well

indicators.note: the letters are found inside the phrase that follows, running across the word gap

parts.note: the letters sit inside, spanning the two words

explanation.surface: Someone tumbled down a well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fell' reads as the past of fall; it is the verb meaning cut down a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: To hew is to chop with an axe, so to fell a tree is to hew it.

clue.text: Goes ahead and does what killer does

definitions.meaning: first meaning: comes earlier in time than something else
second meaning: hunts prey, as a predator does

explanation.surface: Someone goes ahead and commits a murder.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a back-formation from predator, meaning to hunt and eat other animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that predates another comes before it in time; a hunting animal predates when it preys on others.

clue.text: Spot almost perfect escape route from tunnel

indicators.note: almost all of the word is kept, its final letter falling away

parts.note: a blot is a spot or stain, here without its last letter
whole means complete and undamaged

explanation.surface: A prisoner picks out a nearly flawless way to break out of a tunnel.
explanation.walkthrough: The escaping thing is air or smoke, not a prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: A blowhole is a vent letting air or gas out of an underground tunnel.

clue.text: A sport, one that initially backed car maker

indicators.note: going backwards means the whole string is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written
to sport with something is to toy or play with it

indicators.note: initially points to the start of each of the two words before it, so only their first letters are taken

parts.note: the first letter of the word
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A punter bets on a sporting outcome, sponsored by a car firm.
explanation.walkthrough: A, TOY, O and T join and are then written backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Toyota is a Japanese company that manufactures cars.
